result.summary: A list of transformation tales is given as a preface (Daphnis, Scython, Celmus, Crocus and Smilax, the Curetes). The Minyeides react to the previous story, some doubting it, and then Alcithoë takes her turn, naming tales she will skip before promising a novelty.

scenes.title: Alcithoë passes over old tales
scenes.summary: After a list of transformations, the sisters react to the last tale. Alcithoë, weaving, lists well-known changes she will not tell and promises something new.

notable_quotes.reason: A brief, memorable aphorism on the power of lovers' anger.

analysis.text: Ovid uses a rapid catalogue of metamorphoses to show how many such tales exist, while the sisters' storytelling serves to avoid honoring Bacchus.
Storytelling while spinning and weaving reflects a typical domestic setting for women's work in the ancient world.

fun_facts.text: Adamant, the hard substance Celmus becomes, was a legendary unbreakable material, and the root of the English word diamond.

language_notes.text: Adamant is a legendary unbreakable substance, often steel or diamond; here Celmus becomes this hard, unyielding material.
The Curetes were said to have sprung from rain showers; in myth they were attendants who guarded the infant Jupiter.
The sisters doubt Bacchus's divinity, saying real gods can do all things but he is not one of them. The remark is a skeptical jab at the god.
Running the shuttle through the warp means passing the weft thread through the lengthwise threads of the loom while she speaks.
Alcithoë's phrase 'I keep silence' is a rhetorical device of declining to tell a story while actually mentioning it.
Crocus and Smilax were lovers turned into flowers; the crocus plant and a climbing vine, smilax.

context_notes.text: Alcithoë and her sisters, the daughters of Minyas, refuse to honor Bacchus and spin and weave during his festival, telling stories to pass the time.
Celmus was an attendant of the infant Jupiter on Crete who, according to Ovid, was turned to adamant for offending the god.

literary_notes.text: By declaring she will not tell these tales, Alcithoë recites them anyway, showing learning and building anticipation for her new story.
This general maxim about lovers' grief turns the shepherd's fate into a broad truth about love.
Addressing the transformed Celmus directly gives the catalogue a personal, rhetorical tone.
